title: Dynamics of blood Taurine concentration and its correlation with nutritional and physiological status during the fattening period of Japanese black cattle

sections.abstract:
Taurine, biosynthesized from methionine or cysteine in the liver, plays a crucial regulatory role in bile acid conjugation, antioxidant effects, and glucose and cholesterol metabolism. This may influence the metabolic changes associated with fat accumulation in beef cattle. However, the physiological role of taurine in this species has not been fully elucidated. In this study, we explored the physiological role of taurine in Japanese Black steers (Bos taurus) in different phases during the fattening period. To examine the correlation among plasma taurine concentrations, various physiological parameters, and genes related to taurine synthesis in the liver, we used biopsied liver tissues, blood samples, and rumen fluids collected from 21 steers at three different stages, i.e., early (T1; 13 mo of age), middle (T2; 20 mo of age), and late (T3; 28 mo of age) phases. Additionally, to investigate the regulatory mechanisms underlying the expression profile of taurine synthesis genes, primary bovine hepatocytes obtained from 4-wk-old Holstein calves were treated with palmitate, oleate, acetate, propionate, or β-hydroxybutyrate (BHBA). Plasma taurine and cholesterol concentrations significantly ( P < 0.001) increased in the T2 phase, which is potentially attributable to increased energy intake and assimilation induced by increased intake of concentrated feed. Cysteine-sulfinic acid decarboxylase (CSAD) expression significantly increased ( P < 0.01) in T2 than in other phases. The expression levels of cysteine dioxygenase type 1 (CDO1) and cholesterol 7 alpha-hydroxylase (CYP7A1) were significantly higher ( P < 0.05) in T2 than in T3; moreover, the CDO1/glutamate-cysteine ligase catalytic subunit (GCLC) ratio was higher ( P < 0.05) in T2 than in T1. Plasma taurine concentrations were positively correlated with plasma methionine ( r = 0.51; P < 0.05) and total cholesterol ( r = 0.56; P < 0.05) concentrations at T2. Relative CDO1 mRNA expression was upregulated in cultured bovine hepatocytes treated with oleate and propionate, whereas it was downregulated upon acetate treatment. These findings indicate that the increase in plasma taurine concentrations in the T2 phase is associated with changes in lipid and methionine metabolism in Japanese Black steers.

Keywords: fattening period, Japanese Black cattle, lipid metabolism, taurine
sections.introduction:
Japanese Black cattle, renowned for their exceptionally marbled beef, are maintained on a high-concentrate, low-roughage diet during the fattening period to optimize marbling ( Gotoh et al., 2018 ; Smith et al., 2018 ). This dietary strategy, tailored to gradually increase the concentrate-to-roughage ratio, is adopted from approximately 11 mo of age until slaughter. This group of cattle exhibits a much longer fattening period compared with other breeds ( Hozáková et al., 2020 ; Pritchard et al., 2021 ); hence, we aimed to explore their metabolic shifts and lipid metabolism in the liver. Previously, we reported the influence of dietary management during the finishing period on the physiological and metabolic changes ( Kim et al., 2022 ).

Taurine, a multi-functional β-amino acid, is ubiquitous in cellular environments and contains a unique sulfur-containing sulfonic acid group that distinguishes it from standard α-amino acids. Its physiological roles include bile acid conjugation ( Garbutt et al., 1971 ), osmotic balance ( Hussy et al., 2000 ), antioxidative activity ( Thirupathi et al., 2018 ), glucose modulation ( Murakami et al., 2022 ), and cholesterol metabolism ( Chen et al., 2012 ). Hepatic taurine synthesis comprises a 3-step pathway: initially, in the methionine cycle, methionine is converted into homocysteine through the intermediates S-Adenosylmethionine and S-Adenosylhomocysteine ( Finkelstein, 1990 ); the methionine cycle is followed by the transsulfuration pathway that includes the transformation of homocysteine into cystathionine and cysteine via the enzymes cystathionine beta-synthase (CBS) and cystathionine gamma-lyase (CTH; Stipanuk, 2004 ), concurrently producing H 2 S to combat oxidative stress and inflammation ( McBean, 2012 ); finally in cysteine dioxygenase pathway, CDO1 converts cysteine to cysteine sulfonic acid followed by its cysteine-sulfinic acid decarboxylase (CSAD)-mediated conversion to hypotaurine, and generation of taurine ( Huxtable, 1992 ). Cysteine is also pivotal in glutathione (GSH) synthesis; it is converted to γ-glutamylcysteine by the GCLC and glutamate-cysteine ligase modifier subunit before adding glycine to form GSH. A portion of cysteine is allocated to GSH synthesis and the rest is either integrated into proteins or degraded to form taurine ( Meister and Anderson, 1983 ). Taurine biosynthesis is especially important in herbivores, including cattle; contrastingly, carnivores obtain taurine exogenously from their diet ( Spitze et al., 2003 ; Wang et al., 2016 ).

Despite the lack of comprehensive knowledge of the role of taurine in bovine health, its known influence in lowering very low-density lipoprotein and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol concentrations in rodents ( Park and Lee, 1998 ; Chen et al., 2016 ) suggests that taurine influences cholesterol and bile acid secretion from the liver, thereby facilitating lipid digestion and absorption in the gastrointestinal tract. We hypothesize that taurine synthesis and function in beef cattle may be modulated in response to variations in blood metabolites and liver health status throughout the fattening period. In this study, we investigated the changes in taurine metabolism during the fattening period in Japanese Black cattle focusing on its nutritional and physiological implications.
sections.methods:
The animal experiment was conducted at the Hyogo Prefectural Technology Center of Agriculture, Forestry, and Fisheries in Japan. We adhered strictly to the ethical standards established by the Institute of Livestock and Grassland Science (NARO) and the Animal Care and Use Committee of the Hyogo Prefectural Institute of Agriculture, Forestry, and Fisheries, receiving approval under the number H2018-01. Our procedures were in compliance with the ARRIVE guidelines ( https://arriveguidelines.org ).

A cohort of 21 Japanese Black cattle was monitored from the age of 12 mo, with an initial average weight of 335.6 ± 19.8 kg, until they reached 30 mo of age when their average weight was 742.1 ± 49.9 kg. This fattening period was divided into three phases, i.e., early (12 to 14 mo, T1), middle (15 to 22 mo, T2), and late (23 to 30 mo, T3), with formula feed adjusted in each phase to reflect the increasing intake capacity and nutritional needs as the cattle matured, as per the guidelines of the Hyogo Prefectural Technology Center. The nutrient composition of the diet in each phase, feed intake, and growth performance are presented in Table 1 .

Growth performance, feed intake, and nutrient composition of feed in the fattening phases of Japanese Black steers

1 Nutritional composition of the concentrate diet was as follows: T1: DM 87.3%, TDN 71.2%, and CP 15.9%; T2: DM 87.2%, TDN 72.5%, and CP 14.4%; and T3:87.3%, TDN 72.8%, and CP 12.0%. Rice straw: DM 87.8%, TDN 37.7%, CP 4.7%. Kraft pulp feed: DM 76.9%, TDN 51.1%, CP 0.3%. This was also described in our earlier study ( Kim et al., 2022 ).

T1, early fattening phase (age: 13 mo); T2, middle fattening phase (age: 20 mo); T3, late fattening phase (age: 28 mo).

Blood, liver tissue, and ruminal fluid collections were carried out at 13, 20, and 28 mo of age. Liver biopsies were taken from 20, 20, and 19 animals in T1, T2, and T3, respectively, from a location between the right 11th and 12th intercostal space aligned with the line from the right acromion to the tuber coxa. The biopsy site was anesthetized with xylazine. An automatic biopsy gun equipped with a 150-mm needle (ACECUT ACE-141502, DELTA surgical, UK) was used. After the biopsy, the samples were subjected to post-procedure disinfection with 10% povidone-iodine gel. All collected samples were immediately frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80 °C for later RNA extraction. Blood samples were drawn from the jugular vein into heparin-sodium tubes (Venoject II VP-H100K, Terumo, Tokyo, Japan), and rumen fluid samples were collected via oral catheter into sterilized flasks with approximately 200 mL per sample. The analyses of plasma metabolites and rumen volatile fatty acid (VFA)s have been detailed in preceding publications ( Kim et al., 2022 ; Lee et al., 2024 ).

An in vitro experiment was conducted using bovine hepatocytes isolated from a 4-wk-old male Holstein calf, following protocols by Shikida et al. ( Shikida et al., 2023 ). The calf was sourced from a commercial farm in Miyagi, Japan, where it had been nourished on a commercial milk replacer (Calftop EX, Zenrakuren, Tokyo, Japan) with high nutrient specifications (TDN > 103%, CP > 28%, and crude fat > 15%). The milk replacer was offered in buckets, at 9:00 and 16:00 hours, with free access to drinking water. Euthanasia was performed using sodium pentobarbital (25 mg/kg body weight), facilitated by an intravenous injection of sodium pentobarbital in 0.9% NaCl followed by exsanguination. Following euthanasia, a collagenase solution was recirculated within the liver lobes to segregate cells, which were then finely chopped with surgical scissors and immersed in Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle’s Medium (DMEM-High glucose; Gibco, Grand Island, NY, USA) enriched with 100 units/mL penicillin (FUJIFILM Wako Pure Chemical Co., Osaka, Japan) and 20 mM 4-(2-hydroxyethyl)-1-piperazineethanesulfonic acid (HEPES). This preparation was filtered through a 70 μm cell strainer into a 50 mL centrifuge tube and subjected to centrifugation at 163.5 × g for 1 min at 4 °C. Post-supernatant aspiration, the cell pellet was resuspended in the same specified medium. Cell quantification was conducted using a Countess II FL Automated Cell Counter (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA). These cells were then cultured in 24-well plates coated with collagen I-C type (7 × 10 4 cells/cm 2 per well) for 48 h in DMEM-High glucose supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (Gibco, Grand Island, New York, USA), 100 units/mL penicillin, 20 mM HEPES, 1 μM insulin (Sigma-Aldrich Co., Massachusetts, USA), and 1 μM dexamethasone (Sigma-Aldrich Co.). Following 3 washes in fresh medium, an additional 6-h culture period in serum-free medium preceded the introduction of various substrates (palmitate, oleate, BHBA, acetate, or propionate) at concentrations derived from physiological norms of Holstein calves or previous studies ( Jacometo et al., 2016 ; Nakano et al., 2018 ; Nishihara et al., 2020 ). After 24 h of treatment, the cells were gathered for RNA extraction analysis.

The liver specimens or the cultured cells were immersed in 200 μL of RNAiso Plus (TAKARA Bio Inc., Shiga, Japan), then homogenized in liquid nitrogen using a Multibeads shocker (YASUIKIKAI Inc., Osaka, Japan) following the manufacturer’s instructions. Homogenization was performed twice, each time at 2,000 rpm for 10 to 15 seconds. Subsequently, an additional 800 μL of RNAiso Plus was introduced to the mixture at a temperature of 25 °C. The homogenate was then transferred into 1.5 mL microcentrifuge tubes, to which 200 μL of chloroform was added. The resultant mixture was vigorously shaken to ensure thorough mixing before being allowed to settle for 5 min at room temperature. The mixture was centrifuged at 12,000 × g for 15 min at a temperature of 4 °C and the supernatant was carefully collected. This supernatant was then combined with 500 μL of isopropanol, and the solution was again centrifuged under the same conditions to facilitate RNA precipitation. Following the removal of the supernatant, the RNA pellet was washed twice using 75% ethanol chilled to cold temperatures and subsequently dissolved in RNase-free water. The purity and concentration of the obtained total RNA were quantified using a NanoDrop ND-1000 Spectrophotometer V3.7.1 (Thermo Fisher Scientific, MA, USA), measuring absorbance at 230, 260, and 280 nm wavelengths. The quality of RNA, inferred from the A260/A280 ratio, was expected to exceed a value of 1.8, a criterion confirmed through electrophoresis on 1.0% agarose gels. Finally, all RNA samples were stored at -80 °C until further analysis.

Using 500 ng of total RNA, the conversion to complementary DNA (cDNA) was facilitated using the PrimeScript RT Reagent Kit (Takara Bio Inc.). To investigate the relative mRNA expression level of hepatic genes, quantitative real-time PCR (q-RT-PCR) was executed employing the SYBR Premix Ex Taq II (Takara Bio Inc.) on the CFX Connect Real-Time PCR Detection System (BIO-RAD, CA, USA). To determine relative fold changes, the 2 −∆∆CT method was meticulously applied. Normalization of the expression levels of investigated genes was achieved through the geometric mean of 2 housekeeping genes: 18S ribosomal RNA (rRNA) and the vacuolar protein sorting 4 homolog A (VPS4A), which were utilized as internal controls to ensure accuracy and reliability of the results. Information regarding the specific sequences of the primers used is detailed in Supplementary Table S2 .

Statistical analyses were performed using R 4.0.3 software (2020, R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria). Differences in blood metabolite and ruminal VFA concentrations and hepatic gene expressions in the liver among fattening phases were analyzed using a one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s multiple range test. For data with unequal variances, Dunnett’s test was used. The relationship between plasma taurine level and other blood or rumen parameters was assessed by Spearman’s correlation analysis across the fattening phases. All the data used in correlation analysis such as growth performance, rumen fermentation characteristics, blood metabolites, and amino acids were from our previous studies ( Kim et al., 2022 ; Lee et al., 2024 ). The differences in mRNA expression in hepatocytes among the treatments were analyzed using a one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s multiple-range test. Statistical differences were considered significant at P < 0.05.
sections.results:
Figure 1 shows the plasma taurine concentration and its correlation with carcass weight during the fattening period. Taurine increased more than 2-fold from the T1 to T2 phase ( P < 0.01); in the T3 phase, it decreased to the level recorded in T1 ( P < 0.01). Taurine exhibited a positive correlation with carcass weight in T2 ( P < 0.1) and T3 ( P < 0.05); other blood and ruminal parameters were potentially related to plasma taurine concentrations during each phase ( Supplementary Table S1 ). Total cholesterol concentrations were higher in T2 than in T1 and T3 ( P < 0.01). The concentration of methionine was lower in T2 than that in T1 ( P < 0.05). The methionine biosynthesis pathway (KEGG:M00017) was more abundant in T2 than in T1 or T3 ( P < 0.05).

The blood taurine concentration and its correlation with carcass weight during the fattening period. T1, early fattening phase (age: 13 mo); T2, middle fattening phase (age: 20 mo), ); T3, late fattening phase (age: 28 mo). * indicates P < 0.001.

Table 2 lists the correlation coefficients between plasma taurine concentrations and other blood or ruminal parameters detected in T2. Taurine was positively correlated with ruminal propionate ( r = 0.45; P < 0.05), total plasma cholesterol ( r = 0.56; P < 0.01), phospholipid ( r = 0.56; P < 0.05), ALT ( r = 0.48; P < 0.05), and methionine ( r = 0.51; P < 0.05) concentrations, whereas it did not correlate with cysteine concentrations.

The correlations between the blood taurine concentration and physiological parameters in the middle fattening phase of Japanese Black cattle

Figure 2 shows the relative mRNA expression levels of taurine biosynthesis-related genes in liver tissue at each phase. The expression of CSAD was greater in T2 than in T1 and T3 ( P < 0.05) and dropped in T3 ( P < 0.01). The expression of CDO1 was upregulated in T2 ( P < 0.05) compared to T3. The ratio of CDO1 to GCLC was higher in T2 ( P < 0.05) than that in T1. The expression of CTH was upregulated in T2 ( P < 0.05) compared to T3. However, the CBS expression level was not different among the three phases.

The relative expression level of taurine biosynthesis-related genes in the liver of Japanese Black steers during the fattening period. CBS, cystathionine beta-synthase; CTH, cystathionine gamma-lyase; CDO1, cysteine dioxygenase type 1; CSAD, cysteine-sulfinic acid decarboxylase; GCLC, glutamate-cysteine ligase regulatory subunit; T1, early fattening phase (age: 13 mo); T2, middle fattening phase (age: 20 mo); T3, late fattening phase (age: 28 mo). The results are expressed as mean ± standard error of fold changes relative to the baseline mRNA expression in T1. Different letters reflect significant differences between groups ( P < 0.05).

Figure 3 illustrates the relative expression of genes associated with bile acid biosynthesis in the liver during three phases. The expression of CYP7A1 mRNA was higher in T2 ( P < 0.05) than in T3, whereas the ATP-binding cassette, sub-family B member 11 (ABCB11) was upregulated in T1 ( P < 0.05) compared to T3. However, no significant variation in bile acid CoA:amino acid n -acyltransferase (BAAT) expression was detected in different phases.

Relative mRNA expression of bile acids biosynthesis-related genes in the liver of Japanese Black steers during the fattening period. CYP7A1, Cholesterol 7 alpha-hydroxylase; ABCB11, ATP-binding cassette, sub-family B member 11, BAAT: bile acid-CoA:amino acid n -acyltransferase. Gene expression levels were analyzed in 21 Japanese Black steers during their fattening period. T1, early fattening phase (age: 13 mo); T2, middle fattening phase (age: 20 mo); T3, late fattening phase (age: 28 mo). The results are expressed as mean ± standard error of fold changes relative to the baseline mRNA expression in T1. Different letters reflect significant differences between groups ( P < 0.05).

Figure 4 shows the relative CDO1 mRNA expression levels in cultured hepatocytes treated with palmitate, oleate, acetate, propionate, or BHBA. Neither BHBA nor palmitate affect CDO1 expression. Oleate (250 and 500 µM) treatments enhanced the expression of CDO1 mRNA ( P < 0.05) compared to that in the untreated control. Propionate at a concentration of 5 mM increased CDO1 expression ( P < 0.05) compared to that at a lower concentration (2.5 mM) and in the untreated control. Conversely, 17.5 and 35 mM acetate reduced CDO1 expression ( P < 0.05).

Effect of acetate, propionate, BHBA, palmitate, and oleate on the expression of CDO1 mRNA in cultured bovine hepatocytes. Hepatocytes, isolated from one 4-wk-old male Holstein bull calf, were cultured and allowed to proliferate until they reached approximately 80% confluence. Next, these primary hepatocytes were treated with different concentrations of acetate, propionate, beta-hydroxybutyric acid (BHBA), palmitate, or oleate for 24 h, followed by the extraction of total RNA and qRT-PCR analysis of the relative expression of CDO1 mRNA. The results are expressed as mean ± standard error of fold changes relative to the baseline mRNA expression in untreated control cells. Different letters reflect significant differences between groups ( P < 0.05).
sections.discussion:
In this study, the plasma taurine concentration doubled during the middle fattening phase (T2) of Japanese Black cattle compared to the early (T1) and late (T3) fattening phases. This variation is prospectively attributable to the metabolic adaptation to the variable diet formulation adjusted during the fattening stages. Substantial alterations in feed composition and nutrient density affected other blood parameters and hepatic gene expression. Additionally, a positive correlation between the plasma taurine concentration and carcass weight in T2 and T3 was identified, suggesting a relationship between taurine and productivity.

Strict carnivores, such as cats, lack the ability to synthesize taurine in their bodies, and therefore, need to ingest it as an essential nutrient through diet ( Wang et al., 2016 ). Contrastingly, in herbivores, including cattle, taurine is naturally generated from sulfur-containing amino acids, such as methionine and cysteine, via the cysteine-sulfinic acid pathway ( Spitze et al., 2003 ; Wang et al., 2016 ). This process involves the degradation of methionine and homocysteine, leading to the formation of cysteine which serves as an intermediate for the conversion of sulfur into end products such as taurine and sulfate ( Stipanuk and Ueki, 2011 ). In this study, we demonstrated a positive correlation between plasma concentrations of taurine and methionine, the precursor of cysteine, in T2, whereas no correlation was found between plasma cysteine and taurine concentrations at any phase. Hence, taurine synthesis in the bovine liver is more dependent on the availability of methionine than on cysteine itself.

The plasma methionine concentration does not correspond to that of the plasma taurine across the 3 fattening periods. The level of ruminal methionine biosynthesis by rumen microbes can partly explain the amount of methionine entering the liver. In this study, the microbial synthesis of methionine (KEGG: M00017) was upregulated in T2 than in T1, which may be directly linked to the elevated taurine concentrations at T2. To confirm this, it was necessary to measure the methionine concentration in the rumen. To delve deeper into the conversion of methionine to taurine via cysteine generation, we examined the hepatic expression of the genes involved in this pathway. Methionine is transformed into homocysteine via demethylation. The CBS activity initiates the transsulfuration pathway by converting homocysteine to cystathionine ( Conan et al., 2022 ), followed by CTH, which converts cystathionine to cysteine ( Bonifácio et al., 2021 ).

Although the CTH level was markedly elevated in T2 than in T3, the changes in CBS and CTH levels did not completely correspond to the observed fluctuations in taurine concentration across the fattening phases. This disparity implies that the augmentation of taurine concentrations at T2 might be predominantly attributable to the increased plasma methionine concentrations rather than the variations in cysteine abundance or activation of the cysteine synthesis pathway. The positive correlation between plasma taurine and methionine concentrations validated this hypothesis.

Cysteine can be metabolized through various pathways, including those associated with the synthesis of the endogenous antioxidants, glutathione, and taurine. The CDO1 gene plays a crucial role in directing cysteine towards the taurine synthesis pathway by converting it into cysteine-sulfinic acid (CSA; Chen et al., 2023 ). Subsequently, CSAD transforms CSA into hypotaurine, which is further oxidized to taurine. On the other hand, the initial rate-limiting step of glutathione biosynthesis from cysteine is GCL comprising a heavy catalytic subunit known as GCLC ( Lu, 2013 ). In this study, the fluctuations in CDO1 and CSAD levels mirrored the variation in taurine concentrations and contributed to the increased taurine concentration in T2. Conversely, the activity of GCLC, essential for glutathione biosynthesis from cysteine, was not increased in T2. To ascertain the distribution of cysteine conversion to taurine vs. glutathione, the CDO1/GCLC ratio was calculated; intriguingly, this ratio was higher in T2 than in T1. Hence, the T2 phase-specific elevation in taurine concentration is attributed to the preferential conversion of cysteine to taurine, rather than to glutathione, which may be associated with upregulated transcript-level expression of CDO1 and CSAD in the liver.

To determine whether the increased synthesis of taurine in the liver during the T2 phase correlates with dietary changes, expression analysis of CDO1, a key enzyme for taurine biosynthesis, was conducted after in vitro exposure of bovine hepatocytes to BHBA, acetate, and propionate, which are considered to influence to the liver during the middle fattening phase in vivo ( Kim et al., 2022 ).

The transition of diet between the T1 and T2 phases is characterized by an increase in the feed intake. Notably, the adipose tissue and muscle of Japanese Black cattle contain higher concentrations of oleate than those of other breeds ( Sturdivant et al., 1992 ), highlighting the role of oleate metabolism in the liver following increased fat intake.

Excess amounts of oleate cause oxidative stress in liver cells; however, its stimulatory effects on bovine liver cells have not been extensively studied. As the primary monounsaturated fatty acid, oleate contributes to the development and progression of nonalcoholic fatty liver disease ( Jiao et al., 2020 ; Loomba et al., 2021 ). It increases oxidative damage in rat brains, induces oxidative stress in human L02 and HepG2 cell lines ( Yu et al., 2018 ), and causes steatosis in rat BRL-3A cells ( Zhang et al., 2019 ). Supplementation with oleate or its derivative, oleoylethanolamide, has been shown to attenuate HFD-induced hepatic oxidative stress and steatosis in rats ( Giudetti et al., 2021 ). In this study, we observed oleate-stimulated upregulation of CDO1 expression in bovine hepatocytes, suggesting a defensive role for CDO1 against oxidative stress when the bovine liver is exposed to excess fatty acids.

The transition in diet between T1 and T2 resulted in dramatic metabolic shifts in the rumen, specifically with a decrease in acetate and an increase in propionate concentrations ( Kim et al., 2022 ). Our in vitro experiments using bovine hepatocytes revealed that CDO1 mRNA expression was enhanced by propionate exposure in a dose-dependent manner and decreased by acetate. As our results cannot validate the link between VFAs produced in the rumen and the activation of the hepatic taurine synthesis pathway, further studies are needed to comprehensively explore this correlation.

Moreover, we explored the metabolic pathways responsible for bile acid synthesis in the liver with special emphasis on the essential role of taurine in this process. In hepatocytes, bile acids originate from cholesterol. The CYP7A1 gene catalyzes the first step of the conventional pathway of bile acid generation ( Wang et al., 2018 ). During the middle fattening phase (T2) in Japanese Black cattle, dietary adjustments induce increased intake of lipids and boost intramuscular fat accumulation. As indicated in this study, this dietary shift increased plasma cholesterol concentrations and triggered an increase in CYP7A1 activity to enhance bile acid production.

Most bile acids are conjugated with either taurine or glycine before their release into the bile ( Hofmann et al., 2010 ), which reduces their passive reabsorption through biological membranes, enabling the formation of micelles in the intestine that are vital for lipid absorption ( Di Ciaula et al., 2018 ). The BAAT enzyme is essential for this conjugation step ( Kirilenko et al., 2019 ). ABCB11 primarily transports bile acids from hepatocytes to the bile duct ( Zhang et al., 2012 ), showing a distinct preference for taurine-conjugated bile acids; this fact is evident in both humans and rats ( Gerloff et al., 1998 ; Byrne et al., 2002 ; Hayashi et al., 2005 ). Interestingly, in our study, despite dietary changes that led to increased cholesterol and an expected rise in bile acid production during the transition from T1 to T2, the levels of BAAT and ABCB11 did not increase with increasing taurine biosynthesis. Although changes in bile acid concentrations were not examined, these results suggest that increased hepatic taurine biosynthesis may not directly enhance taurine-conjugated bile acids, and further research is needed to confirm this.

Several reports have indicated a role for taurine in lipid metabolism. Taurine-conjugated bile acids are more effective than glycine-conjugated bile acids in the emulsification and solubilization of lipids and facilitate their digestion and absorption ( Wang et al., 2020 , 2022 ). Dietary taurine supplementation reduces peripheral cholesterol, visceral fat, serum total cholesterol, and triglyceride concentrations in broilers ( Zeng et al., 2012 ) and humans ( Martins et al., 2021 ). We detected a positive correlation of taurine with cholesterol and triglyceride concentrations in the T2 phase, suggesting its potential role in supporting active lipid metabolism associated with increased fat intake during this period. Therefore, further research on the role of taurine status in lipid metabolism and a broader analysis of the enzymatic genes responsible for the production of taurine-conjugated bile acids are necessary.

In conclusion, in Japanese Black steers, the plasma taurine concentration was elevated in the middle fattening phase than in the early and late phases, which coincided with the expression profile of the taurine and glutathione synthesis-related genes in the liver. The in vitro results indicated that increased oleate and rumen-derived propionate supply to the liver induced by a shift to increased feed intake may stimulate taurine biosynthesis. Augmented fat intake may exacerbate oxidative stress in the liver and mitigate it by activating taurine synthesis mediated by CDO1. Concurrently, dietary change enhanced plasma total cholesterol and hepatic expression of CYP7A1 mRNA, implying a link between taurine and bile acid function in beef cattle during the fattening period. Further investigations can provide a deeper understanding of the role of taurine in beef cattle.
